tagline: Forests, lakes and the midnight sun
overview:
Sweden stretches nearly 1,600 kilometers from the Baltic Sea in the south to well above the Arctic Circle in the north, making it the largest country in northern Europe and about the size of California. Forest covers roughly two-thirds of the land, and there are close to 100,000 lakes. Stockholm, the capital, is built across fourteen islands where a great lake meets the sea, stitched together by bridges and ferries.

About 10.5 million people live in Sweden, most of them in the milder south. Swedish is the national language, and the Sami people of the north speak Sami languages. Sweden is a constitutional monarchy: a king serves as ceremonial head of state while an elected parliament called the Riksdag governs. The country is known for a strong welfare system, long parental leave, and design that favors simple, useful things. Swedish inventions, from the safety match to the three-point seatbelt, have traveled far beyond its borders.
landAndNature: The Scandinavian Mountains run along the Norwegian border, rising to Kebnekaise at about 2,100 meters and dotted with small glaciers. Below them lie the tundra and marshes of Lapland, then vast spruce and pine forests, and finally farmland and beech woods in the far south. Sweden's coast is fringed with archipelagos; the Stockholm archipelago alone counts some 30,000 islands and rocky skerries. North of the Arctic Circle the sun does not set for weeks in summer and barely rises in winter, when the northern lights ripple green overhead. Moose, lynx, wolverines and brown bears live in the forests, and reindeer herds are tended by Sami herders.
peopleAndCulture: Swedes take a daily coffee break called fika, pausing with a cinnamon bun and company rather than rushing. Food runs from meatballs with lingonberry jam to pickled herring, crispbread and, in the north, the famously pungent fermented fish surströmming. Midsummer in late June is the biggest celebration, with flower crowns, a leafy maypole and dancing outdoors until the sky barely darkens. Saint Lucia's Day in December brings children in white robes carrying candles and singing at dawn. A legal right of public access lets anyone walk and camp in the countryside. Ice hockey and soccer are the main sports, and Swedish songwriters shape pop music worldwide.
history: Sweden's Viking Age seafarers sailed east down Russian rivers to Constantinople and traded as far as Baghdad. Christianity arrived around the year 1000, and by the 1300s Sweden had joined Denmark and Norway in the Kalmar Union, breaking away under Gustav Vasa in 1523. In the 1600s Sweden became a great military power around the Baltic before losing most of those lands, and Finland passed to Russia in 1809. Still a poor farming country in the 1800s, it sent more than a million emigrants to America. Sweden stayed out of both world wars and used the peace to build industry and a generous welfare state. It joined the European Union in 1995 and NATO in 2024.
funFacts: Sweden has about 100,000 lakes, and a right of public access lets anyone walk, swim or camp on most land.
Alfred Nobel, a Swedish chemist who invented dynamite, left his fortune to create the Nobel Prizes.
The three-point seatbelt was invented at Volvo in 1959, and the patent was given away free to save lives.
Sweden burns much of its household waste for heat and electricity, and imports rubbish from other countries as fuel.
Swedes celebrate a cinnamon bun day every October 4, honoring the country's most beloved pastry.
